Download pixal3d_multiview_int8_convrot.safetensors~5.2 GB 

Place in: ComfyUI/models/diffusion_models/3D

 Load CLIP Vision

Download dino_v3_L_naf_fp32.safetensors~1.1 GB 

Place in: ComfyUI/models/clip_vision

 Load VAE (two files)

Download trellis_2_shape_vae_bf16.safetensors~1.0 GB 

Download trellis_2_texture_vae_bf16.safetensors~0.9 GB 

Place in: ComfyUI/models/vae

 Remove Background Pixaroma

Download birefnet.safetensors~424 MB 

Place in: ComfyUI/models/background_removal

One file. The four Cut out the background nodes all use it, and it is only loaded once.

 After placing the files, restart ComfyUI or refresh model lists using the R shortcut.

nodes.title: What each node does
widgets_values:
{"version":1,"content":"

WHAT EACH NODE DOES

The colour of a node tells you what kind of node it is. Nothing here needs changing except the blue ones.

 Models to download

Orange. Each one needs a file from the list in the other note.

  • Load Diffusion Model (Pixal3D Multi-View) - The model that turns the pictures into a 3D shape.
  • Load CLIP Vision (DINOv3) - Reads the pictures so the model understands what it is looking at.
  • Load VAE (shape) - Turns the model's output into geometry.
  • Load VAE (texture) - Turns the model's output into colours.
  • Cut out the background - Cuts the subject away from its background. One per view, all using the same file.

 The numbers you set

Blue, and numbered. These are the only nodes you have to touch.

  • 1. Front view - looks at you - The subject facing the camera.
  • 2. Back view - you see the back - The subject with its back to the camera.
  • 3. Left view - looks LEFT - Taken from the subject's left. In the picture it faces the left edge.
  • 4. Right view - looks RIGHT - Taken from the subject's right. In the picture it faces the right edge.
  • 5. Which views do you have? - Four switches: Front, Back, Left, Right. Click one to turn that view off and the model works from whatever is left. A switched-off view is skipped entirely, so it costs you nothing. Any combination runs, even a single picture, and you do not have to keep the front one.
  • 6. Seed (drives all four samplers) - Same seed, nearly the same result. Change it for a different attempt.

 Picture prep

Slate. These run by themselves.

  • Centre and crop to 1024 x 1024 - Puts the subject in the middle of a square frame. One per view.
  • Front / Back / Left / Right - what the model sees - Shows the cut-out view that is actually being sent. Check these if a result looks wrong.
  • Read the views - Hands the pictures to the model together, so it builds one shape from all of them.

 The four stages

Teal, purple, red then green. This is the model building the object, and it runs the same way every time.

  • Stage 1 - rough voxel blob - A coarse block shape, shown in the first 3D viewer so you can see the run is alive.
  • Stage 2 - the real shape - Turns the blob into the actual form.
  • Stage 3 - refine the shape - Adds the detail. The upsample node just above it decides how much.
  • Stage 4 - the colours - Works out what colour every part of the surface is.

 After the stages

Amber. The mesh tidy-up, the colours and the save.

  • Free the VRAM - Hands the graphics card's memory back once the colours are worked out, before the mesh work starts.
  • Mesh info (polygon count) - Says how big the raw mesh is.
  • Rebuild the mesh cleanly - Redraws the surface as even triangles.
  • Reduce to 200k triangles - Brings the count down to something an ordinary 3D program can open.
  • Smooth the normals - Softens the shading across the surface.
  • Paint the mesh with the colours - Puts Stage 4's colours onto the mesh points.
  • RESULT - saved to output/3d - The finished model, viewable here and written to disk as a .glb file.

nodes.title: Paint the mesh with the colours
Settings for your card
widgets_values:
{"version":1,"content":"

SETTINGS FOR YOUR GRAPHICS CARD

 This one is built for a small card

Everything here is sized to run on a graphics card with 6 GB of memory. The whole run used at most 5.1 GB of it, so there is room to spare.

The colours are painted onto the mesh points rather than baked into texture images. You get a single finished model with its colours, and the steps that would build separate texture maps are not in this workflow. That is what keeps it inside a small card and finishes in minutes. The colours also come out softer than in the Model + PBR Textures workflows: thin lines, small lettering and small glowing parts blur, because each colour sits on a point of the mesh. For crisp colours use one of the Model + PBR Textures workflows.

It also needs plenty of ordinary system memory, because the model is moved out to the computer's memory whenever the card is full. This run reached about 40 GB of system memory.

 Use the views you have

The model does not need all four. Switch off any view you do not have on the 5. Which views do you have? node and it works from the rest. Any combination runs, down to a single picture.

You do not even have to keep the Front one. With Front off, the first view still switched on becomes the front, and the model is posed to face that way instead, so a back-only run gives you a model whose back is facing forward. Everything still lines up, you just have to turn the result round. Leaving Front on saves you that.

Measured on a 6 GB RTX 2060, same subject, same seed. The closeness number says how near that result is to the four-view one, where 1.00 would be identical.

Views switched onCloseness to all four
Front only0.09
Front + Back (opposite each other)0.57
Front + Left (a quarter turn apart)0.70
Front + Back + Left0.75
All four1.00

The jump that matters is getting to three. Three views and four come out close, so a symmetrical subject can stop at three. Two views is where the shape starts drifting, and from one the model is inventing most of the object.

If you only have two, make them 90 degrees apart rather than front and back. Two opposite views tell the model nothing about how deep the subject is.

Front and back scored 0.57 against 0.70 for front and a side, and it came out 8% thinner. It also left a far rougher surface: about eight times as many holes in the mesh as any other combination here.

On a small card the number of views also changes the time. Each view is read separately before the shape is built, and on a card this size that reading is the single longest part of the run. Measured across six runs it costs about 36 seconds per view, so switching one off is worth roughly that much. Everything after the views is the same work whatever you give it.

 The three numbers that decide the speed

Everything else in the workflow can stay as it is. Each row says which node to look for.

SettingNode on the canvasFasterThis workflowMore detail
Upsample resolutionUpsample the shape102410241536
Remesh resolutionRebuild the mesh cleanly256512768
TrianglesReduce to N triangles100,000200,000700,000

The upsample resolution is the biggest one. It is already at its lowest setting here. Raising it to 1536 keeps small details more often and makes the run longer; with the rebuild raised to 768 as well, round surfaces show small flat facets. Do not go above 1536: the node allows 2048, but in testing it made the mesh messier, with about twice as many broken edges and three times as many loose bits, and its details were no closer to the pictures.

The remesh resolution and the triangle count are the mesh tidy-up afterwards. Lower them if the end of the run feels slow; raise them if the surface looks too coarse.

 Measured run time

On a 6 GB RTX 2060 with all four views on, this workflow took between 6 minutes 10 seconds and 7 minutes 22 seconds across several runs. Most of that spread is the models being moved in and out of the card rather than anything you set, so times will wander a little on a card this size.

The Stage 1 result viewer fills in early with a rough blob, which tells you the run is alive. The finished model arrives in the RESULT viewer at the end and is written to output/3d.

 If a run stops partway or ComfyUI disappears

This workflow asks for close to everything a 6 GB card has. The highest reading taken during a run was 5.1 GB, and Windows itself, your browser and any other open program are already using part of the card before ComfyUI starts. On the machine this was measured on that was about 1.6 GB before a single model loaded.

When the total goes over what the card has, the display driver can reset itself and ComfyUI closes with no error message. If that happens:

  • Close other windows that use the graphics card, especially browser tabs with video or 3D in them.
  • Start ComfyUI again and run it once more. It is not a broken workflow, it is the card running out of room.
  • Switching off a view you do not need lowers what the run asks for as well as making it quicker.

 What makes a good set of pictures

  • Same subject, same pose, same lighting in every picture.
  • The same distance every time, so the subject is the same size in each one.
  • A plain background. The workflow cuts it out anyway, but a busy one confuses the cut-out.
  • Renders from a turnaround work best. Photographs work too, as long as you move a quarter turn around the subject each time.

 Left and right are the part people get wrong

The names are about where the camera is standing, not which way the subject is turned. Stand on someone's left and look at them, and their face points off to the left of your picture.

SlotWhat the picture should show
frontThe subject looks at you
leftThe subject looks to the LEFT edge of the frame
backYou see its back
rightThe subject looks to the RIGHT edge of the frame

Get these the wrong way round and the shape still builds, because most subjects are close to symmetrical, but anything on one side only ends up on the wrong side.

 Why Free VRAM is in the workflow

The Free VRAM node sits after the colours are worked out, the last step that needs the big model. It hands the card's memory back before the mesh rebuild, which also runs on the graphics card and needs room of its own.
